data.title: Romance Scammers Use Mississippi Man’s Stolen Photos To Drain About $1,400,000 From Victims
data.description:
Romance scammers have used a Mississippi man’s stolen photos to fool victims out of roughly $1.4 million.

Hunter Bigham, a sales executive and father of three in Tupelo, is not the scammer, reports The Independent.

For more than eight years, fraudsters have used his pictures to build hundreds of fake profiles.

The scammers often cast him as a widowed oil rig worker or geologist.

The Associated Press found 177 Facebook accounts using his photos under the name Henry Clerk alone.

Victims from the U.S., Spain, Venezuela and Hong Kong have tracked him down.

Up to 15 victims contacted Bingham in a day at the peak.

Some have threatened him and his family.

One cancer survivor lost $75,000 to a scammer who claimed to be Bigham’s identical twin.

She later wrote to him in a 2019 message.

“Hunter, I fell in love. And I was a fool. You are now the only one who knows the extent of it. I am retired and have no way to replenish this money.”

Bigham says he reported the fake profiles to Facebook, but the platform repeatedly told him they did not violate its community standards.

He also filed a report with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center.

The agency told him there was little it could do, he says.

Meta told the AP it removed four accounts he recently reported and is investigating his case.

The company also said it removed over 179 million accounts, pages and groups for misrepresenting identity in the first half of 2026.

Bigham places the blame on the platforms.

“I hold the most responsibility for the platforms. They could stop this today.”

data.title: PNC Bank Insider Accused of Stealing $86,107 From the Lender and Spending It on Gambling
data.description:
A PNC Bank supervisor has been accused of stealing more than $86,000 from her employer and spending it on gambling.

Jacqueline Clinton, 48, of Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, allegedly misused her position as Bank Reconcilements Operations Supervisor at PNC Bank to make false credit adjustments and direct the money to her personal account, the Allegheny County District Attorney’s Office says.

Prosecutors say Clinton made ten fraudulent credit adjustments between May and August of 2026, pulling a total of $86,107.66 from the bank’s Regulation E Disputes General Ledgers, the internal accounting accounts used by banks and other financial institutions to track disputed funds, provisional credits, network chargeback recoveries, and fraud losses. Regulation E is a set of rules that outline procedures that banks and other financial institutions should handle disputes.

Those funds were meant to be distributed to client accounts for refunds, credit or deposits.

The district attorney’s office says her bank records show ATM withdrawals at casinos and transactions on online gambling sites. Clinton made mobile transfers to herself, according to Allegheny County District Attorney’s Office.

Clinton faces charges of theft by unlawful taking, receiving stolen property, access device fraud, misapplication of entrusted property and unlawful use of a computer.

A preliminary hearing is scheduled for February 4th of 2027.

data.title: Massachusetts Health Firm To Hand Out up to $2,000 per Person To Settle Data Beach That Exposed Names, Social Security Numbers and More
data.description:
Patients affected by a data breach at a Massachusetts community health center can claim up to $2,000 for documented losses or an estimated $40 payment, plus two years of medical identity monitoring, under a $750,000 class action settlement.

The agreement resolves allegations that DotHouse Health failed to safeguard patient information during a 2022 cyberattack, according to the settlement administrator’s portal.

The breach exposed the data of about 190,000 people, including names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers and medical details.

The notice class covers roughly 145,000 people who were sent letters in July 2025.

“If you incurred actual, documented out-of-pocket losses due to the Data Incident, you can get back up to $2,000.00. The losses must have occurred between October 31, 2022, and January 29, 2027.”

In lieu of the cash payment or documented losses, the settlement class members can also claim pro rata payments of about $40.

The settlement is open to Massachusetts residents and others who choose to take part.

Claims must be filed by January 29th of 2027.

A final approval hearing is set for January 19th of 2027 in Suffolk County Superior Court.

DotHouse denies any wrongdoing.

The fund will cover administration, attorneys’ fees of up to $250,000 and service awards before payments are distributed.

Two years of CyEx Medical Shield Complete monitoring is also available, valued at about $179 per year.

Those eligible can submit claims online or by mail using the Login ID and PIN from their notice.

data.title: Wisconsin Retiree Loses More Than $400,000 in Gold Courier Scam, Even After Her Bank Questioned Her Cash Withdrawals
data.description:
A Wisconsin retiree has lost more than $400,000 of her retirement savings to scammers who convinced her that handing over gold would protect her money.

The woman, identified only as Mary, clicked a pop-up bearing her financial advisor’s logo that locked her computer, reports WFSB.

Callers posing as her investment company, the sheriff’s office, the FBI and the Federal Trade Commission told her that her account had been hacked.

She was also told she was a suspect in weapons dealing and money laundering.

Mary spent $131,208 on 24 gold coins.

A courier collected the coins from her in a fast food parking lot after an imposter posing as the Better Business Bureau arranged the pickup.

Employees at her bank and at the business that sold her the gold questioned the large cash withdrawals, but she kept making excuses.

She was also instructed to buy Bitcoin and thousands of dollars in gift cards as the fraud continued for three months.

It ended when she called her supposed Better Business Bureau contact and found the number had been disconnected.

Says Lisa Schiller of the Wisconsin Better Business Bureau,

“The extent was unprecedented. I mean, this is probably the largest amount of money loss that we’ve had reported in one single scam.”

Local police say the investigation is ongoing and no arrests have been made.

Says Robin Jacobs of the Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions,

“Hang up your phone or shut down your computer, because once you engage with them, you go down the rabbit hole with them and it’s very hard to disengage at that point, psychologically.”

data.title: PNC Bank Partners With Coinbase To Enable USDC Stablecoin Payments for Institutional and Corporate Customers
data.description:
A major US bank has started letting corporate clients receive stablecoin payments.

PNC Bank says it is making incoming USDC payments available to eligible corporate and institutional panking clients, powered by Coinbase Payment products on the Ethereum blockchain. Coinbase Payments, offered by crypto exchange Coinbase, is a stablecoin payment solution built for commerce platforms.

The payments are converted automatically 1-to-1 into US dollars and deposited into a designated PNC account.

The bank says the service is meant to give businesses faster access to funds and greater efficiency on cross-border transactions.

PNC is initially offering the service on a limited basis to eligible clients as part of a pilot program.

It builds on the bank’s existing relationship with Coinbase.

Says Tom Lang, head of Treasury Management Product and Operations at PNC Bank,

“Our clients are continually looking at new ways to interact and transact with customers, suppliers and business partners. This solution gives us an opportunity to support our customers with innovative capabilities, backed by the banking experience, risk management and expertise clients expect from PNC.”

Says Alec Lovett, head of Infrastructure Products at Coinbase,

“Stablecoins are modernizing how businesses move money by making payments faster, more efficient and more global. Our work with PNC shows how leading banks and trusted digital asset infrastructure come together to let corporate clients take advantage of this technology.”

data.title: New Jersey Repeat Mail Fraudster Charged With Targeting $12,000,000 From Bank and Mailing 36,000 Fake Invoices to Schools
data.description:
A New Jersey man who has served two prison terms for mail scams has been charged again with trying to claim $12 million from a bank and billing schools for books they never ordered.

Robert Armstrong, 56, of Turnersville, has been charged with bank fraud and mail fraud, reports NJ.com.

Federal authorities allege he used fake documents, including a power of attorney, to go after about $12 million in unclaimed funds tied to a 2003 hedge fund investment.

Investigators say the bank sent him a $2,806,524 cashier’s check that he deposited at a branch in Sewell on November 19th, 2025, but the bank declined the deposit because it could not verify the funds.

Armstrong also allegedly filed a claim for $9,251,641.71 with Texas, which denied it.

Postal Inspector Michael Marro Jr. alleges Armstrong paid for five bulk mailings of more than 36,000 fake book invoices to schools across the US and Canada between February and August of 2026.

Marro wrote in the complaint that the invoices school officials provided were

“nearly identical to the ones previously recovered during a prior investigation of Armstrong in 2014.”

Armstrong had deposited 43 checks of $263 each, totaling $11,309, when he was charged.

His first prison term, in late 2015, came from a school invoice scam that brought in $612,774, and a 2020 sentence followed a medical supply invoice scam that brought in $214,495.

Armstrong was charged on October 30th and arrested on November 4th, and he remains in federal detention in Philadelphia.

data.title: Missouri and Kansas Brothers Convicted in Texas of $240,000,000 Cattle Fraud Scheme
data.description:
Federal prosecutors have secured convictions against two brothers for running a $240 million cattle investment scam that defrauded thousands of investors across the country.

Joshua Robert Link of Strafford, Missouri, and Jason Allen Link of Herington, Kansas, were found guilty on charges including wire fraud conspiracy, wire fraud and money laundering after a six-day trial in Fort Worth, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas.

The scheme centered on Agridime, which sold contracts promising individual cattle for $2,000 each but instead diverted the money to pay earlier investors, cover operating costs and fund personal luxuries.

Says U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould,

“These defendants preyed directly on Main Street Americans who believed they were investing in cattle contracts. Instead of building a legitimate cattle business, the Link brothers ran a high-tech Ponzi scheme, siphoning away hard-earned life savings to build luxury retreats and line their own pockets. Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: this office will fiercely defend hard-working citizens from predatory fraudsters and ensure that those who exploit investors are held fully accountable under the law.”

Prosecutors showed the brothers overstated cattle holdings to obtain loans and paid themselves millions in salaries and commissions while shorting investors on actual animals delivered.

“Court documents indicate that over 2,200 individual victims located throughout the United States paid Agridime for specific individual heads of cattle, pursuant to a cattle purchase contract based on fraudulent misrepresentations caused by the defendants.

In total, from January 2021 through December 2023, Agridime collected over $240 million based on fraudulent misrepresentations made in public and private advertising statements…”

Sentencing is scheduled for March 4th, 2027.

data.title: Judge Allows Trump’s $10,000,000,000 Defamation Lawsuit Against BBC to Proceed
data.description:
A federal judge is allowing President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward over an edited clip of his January 6th speech.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz in Florida denied the BBC’s motion to dismiss the defamation per se claim but granted dismissal of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act count, reports NBC News.

The lawsuit centers on a spliced segment from Trump’s January 6th, 2021, speech that combined three quotes from two sections and delivered almost an hour apart into what appeared to be one quote in which Trump urged supporters to march with him and “fight like hell.

The parts left out included a section where Trump said he urged supporters to demonstrate peacefully. The edited speech aired in a BBC “Panorama” documentary shortly before Trump won the 2024 presidential election. A leaked internal BBC memo pointed to the edits as evidence of possible political bias, triggering a public relations crisis and prompting the resignations of senior executives.

President Donald Trump called the ruling a “huge victory” and wrote on social media, “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!”

The BBC had admitted the edit created a mistaken impression and apologized to Trump, but it denies being liable for defamation

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster was surprised by the decision but respects the court’s authority and remains confident in its position.

data.title: New York Man Sentenced in Arizona to 121 Months for Laundering Elder Fraud Proceeds
data.description:
Federal prosecutors have secured a 121-month prison term against a New York resident convicted of laundering nearly $1 million taken from elderly victims in a phishing scam network.

Ivan Wilbur Seales, 58, a New York resident and citizen of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, was also ordered to pay approximately $855,000 in restitution, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona.

Seales retained a share of the stolen funds and laundered the remainder through shell companies, cryptocurrency transfers, cash withdrawals and offshore accounts.

The underlying scheme used fake pop-ups and emails impersonating banks, Apple, Microsoft, Geek Squad, PayPal and an antivirus firm to trick victims into believing they owed or had received erroneous payments.

Victims were instructed to send their own money to the scammers under the false claim that they were returning over-refunded amounts.

“Victims were also lied to and informed that their bank accounts had been hacked or were compromised. At least one victim was told his account was linked to child pornography. To further the scam, the fraudsters directed the victims to transfer their money to various locations to ‘protect’ their accounts or to ‘catch’ the scammers.”

The United States Postal Inspection Service and New York State Police led the investigation into the case, numbered 24-CR-0419-TUC-SHR.

data.title: Huntington Bank Customer Loses $9,000 After Spoofed Caller Has Her Transfer Money at a Branch
data.description:
A Huntington Bank customer has lost $9,000 after a caller posing as a bank employee had her transfer the money at a branch while she was traveling.

The Michigan resident, who asked not to be identified, received the call while out of state, reports ABC12.

The caller identified herself as Huntington Bank employee Ellen Caldwell and said the customer’s account had been hit with fraudulent activity.

The number on the phone appeared to belong to the bank, and the caller told her to move money out through Zelle or a wire transfer.

Says the fraudster,

“We are thinking somebody within the system, in the company, is doing this…

She said your money won’t be touched. We are just going to try to see who is taking this out.”

The woman went to a Huntington branch in that other state and completed two transfers totaling $9,000, one to Bank of America and one to PNC Bank.

Says the victim,

“There was the Huntington name, the Huntington correct number; we called that number back. The person that took me to the bank called the number back while we were standing outside the bank and it was Huntington.”

Similar scams have been reported against Huntington Bank customers in the Cleveland area and in other parts of the country.

The victim says she should have been told earlier that her account had been compromised.

“They are not letting anyone know, because my account was compromised in May and September. I should have been notified.”

She is working with a Huntington branch in Saginaw in hopes of getting the money back.

“To me, they are making it seem like it’s your fault, when the security breach is on their end.”

A Huntington spokesperson says the bank cannot comment on an individual account.

Says the spokesperson,

“Huntington takes fraud concerns seriously and carefully reviews every reported instance based on the facts and circumstances involved.”

The bank reminds customers never to share passwords or sensitive financial information and to slow down and verify unexpected requests before sending money.
